Seton Hall health faculty highlight AI research and professional development at conferences
Faculty from Seton Hall University’s School of Health and Medical Sciences shared their research and expertise at national and international conferences this year, connecting with colleagues across disciplines as the new academic year begins, according to an Aug. 26 announcement.
Artificial intelligence and simulation were central themes in faculty presentations. At the International Meeting on Simulation in Healthcare in January in San Antonio, Lisa Sheikovitz and Alicia MacGregor from the M.S. in Occupational Therapy program presented research on a tool for measuring occupational therapy students’ self-efficacy through simulation. They also discussed applications of artificial intelligence in creating realistic patient cases and tools for learner feedback.
Jessica Dunn from the Doctor of Physical Therapy program participated as part of an interdisciplinary team at the American Physical Therapy Association Combined Sections Meeting in February to develop a course on integrating artificial intelligence into physical therapy education. Angela Lis presented posters about AI use in evidence-based practice education and interprofessional simulation, while Lorene Cobb presented research on surf therapy for children with developmental disabilities co-authored with Jerry-Thomas Monaco and third-year students. Cobb also served as co-chair of the APTA Academy of Pediatrics Movement System Committee.
M.S. in Physician Assistant faculty contributed to professional meetings throughout spring. Abby Saunders addressed bias mitigation efforts at the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, while Vanessa Rodriguez presented student-directed neuroscience teaching methods at another conference. Jurga Marshall discussed AI-powered avatars for patient care training at the American Academy of Physician Associates Annual Conference, where she also supported student researchers Michelle Inga and Sarah Mohan George under advisor Michelle McWeeney.
Research by Master of Healthcare Administration faculty Patrick Bernet and Jeffrey Ritter evaluated AI responses to health administration questions using both student preferences and objective benchmarks; their work was invited for publication following its presentation at a June meeting.
Michael La Fountaine, associate dean of academic affairs and research, said, “Health professions education continues to evolve alongside advances in research, technology and clinical practice. Our faculty bring what they learn through scholarship, collaboration and professional leadership back to their programs, helping ensure that students are learning from the latest research and approaches and are prepared for the changing environments in which they will practice.”
